narrative.title: Why Kelsey?
narrative.highlight: Field sales in healthcare AI is won with hustle, trust, and clinical credibility. I am a competitive, coachable, entrepreneurial outlier who wins on the phone and face to face. I won client trust owning institutional accounts at Goldman Sachs, earned clinical credibility training in the ER as a licensed EMT, and proved my hustle in bilingual door-to-door territory outreach.
narrative.body:
My career started in client relationship management and new business development. My longstanding interest in medicine led me to earn my EMT license, where training in the field and ER alongside clinicians gave me firsthand insight into clinical practice and point-of-care workflows. I saw how much of a physician's time went to documentation instead of patient care. That experience clarified how I wanted to make an impact in healthcare by helping bring innovative tools and technology to the physicians who make treatment decisions, so they can work more effectively and efficiently and patients get the care they need, and help fix healthcare!

Although I have not held a sales title, I bring a proven track record of prospecting, sourcing new business, and retaining high-value accounts, alongside firsthand healthcare experience. At Goldman Sachs, I owned approximately 20 multi-million-dollar accounts and kept 100% of them while solving complex client needs. Through 18 months of volunteer Spanish-language territory outreach, I knocked doors, approached people in public, followed leads, and made phone calls, on a few days hitting up to 100 cold touch points and many times hitting 10 appointments a day. I overcame objections and generated more than 50% of new commitments through referrals. My EMT training strengthened my clinical understanding and experience collaborating with healthcare professionals, preparing me to communicate clinical information effectively, engage physicians, qualify accounts, schedule demos, and drive revenue growth as part of a high-performing team. I hunt new business, and I do not wait for leads to come to me.

startStories.title: Up to 100 Cold Touch Points in a Day
startStories.teaser: 18 months of door-to-door and public outreach in Spanish across three states, on a few days hitting up to 100 cold touch points and many times hitting 10 appointments a day.
startStories.body:
For 18 months I did volunteer outreach in a Spanish-speaking territory across Nebraska, Iowa, and South Dakota. On a 13-hour daily schedule, I knocked doors, approached people in public, followed leads, and made phone calls, on a few days hitting up to 100 cold touch points and many times hitting 10 appointments a day. I did pre-call research and planning before each day and reviewed my results after it. Most people said no, and I kept going.

In Field SDR terms, that is high-volume cold outreach, prospect research, appointment setting, and overcoming rejection every day. I met my weekly goals. I will bring that same volume to cold calls and walk-ins at DFW private practices and turn it into scheduled appointments.

startStories.title: 1 Gatekeeper Who Shut Everyone Out
startStories.teaser: One community leader with influence over a large network had turned away every rep before me. He became our best source of referrals.
startStories.body:
In the same territory, one community leader had influence over a large network of local families, and he had shut out every rep before me. I needed a different angle. I got to know his wife first, learned he missed playing soccer, and organized a recurring pickup game. Over time he became our best source of referrals.

In sales terms, he was the gatekeeper to the account, and his objection was a lack of trust and rapport. I researched him, found the angle, and built the relationship before I asked for anything. More than 50% of my new commitments came through referrals. Healthcare practices run on the same principles: the front desk or office gatekeeper decides who reaches the physician. I will find the right angle, earn access, and turn the first meeting into a scheduled appointment.

startStories.title: 2 a.m. Grit in the Trauma Bay
startStories.teaser: Top 5% of my UT Dallas EMT class. At 2 a.m., the nurses told the other students to follow my lead.
startStories.body:
I finished the UT Dallas EMT program in the top 5% of my cohort. One night around 2 a.m., I was sent to the helipad with two nurses to receive an air ambulance patient. When we got him to the trauma bay, the physician called for someone to shear his clothes to check for injuries. I stepped in while he performed an emergency tracheotomy. I didn't realize the other two EMT students hadn't moved until the nurses told them to follow my lead.

I work best under pressure, and I come prepared for the situation. That is where my clinical credibility comes from. I am familiar with ER documentation of patient care in an EHR, I understand clinical workflows, and I have watched physicians stop to chart before they could get to the next patient. I can talk with a physician or practice manager about ambient AI documentation in terms of their day: less time charting and more time with patients.

startStories.title: 20 Accounts. 100% Retained. Zero Escalations.
startStories.teaser: At Goldman Sachs I owned about 20 multi-million-dollar lending accounts and kept every client happy and on the books.
startStories.body:
At Goldman Sachs I owned about 20 multi-million-dollar corporate lending accounts at a time. The contracts ran 100 to 250+ pages of heavy legal jargon, and I studied them until I could answer client needs in real time. If I gave a client a deadline, I met it, even when that meant working from a plane on Christmas Eve. When teammates were out, I covered their accounts too.

In sales terms, that is account ownership, follow-through, and customer retention. I kept 100% of my book with zero escalations by knowing the details cold and following through every time. As an SDR, the account starts with me. I will qualify it carefully, set clear expectations, hand the Account Executive a clean opportunity, and own every follow-up.

startStories.title: 1 to 13 Clients: 1,200% Growth
startStories.teaser: In 2023 I launched a consulting business with no clients and built it to 13 families through outreach and referrals.
startStories.body:
In 2023 I started a consulting practice helping Dallas families with private school admissions. I had no client list and no marketing budget. I prospected in Dallas parent groups, turned early clients into referral sources, ran a needs assessment with every family, and managed concurrent engagements of 3 to 6 months. I grew the practice to 13 families through outreach and referrals. Each engagement was a large commitment, so I took only a few clients at a time, and 13 was the number that fit my capacity. A couple of families came back for repeat business with a younger child, and one student was admitted to a school with a 15% acceptance rate.

That is new business development from zero: prospecting, qualifying, closing, and earning referrals and repeat business. I will take the same entrepreneurial approach to creating appointments that stick in middle market practice accounts.

startStories.title: Coachable: SQL in 9 Days, $2M Found
startStories.teaser: At Vivint I learned SQL from scratch, delivered executive reporting in 9 days, and found a $2 million revenue opportunity.
startStories.body:
I started at Vivint without knowing SQL and was delivering executive reporting in nine days. Once I was in the data every day, I found seven operational inefficiencies that added up to a $2 million revenue opportunity, built the business case, and presented it to senior leadership. They used it to reallocate resources. At Goldman Sachs I mentored an intern and two struggling teammates by first working out whether each gap was knowledge, confidence, or process.

For a Field SDR, that means I will ramp up quickly on Commure + Athelas middle market products, training, and sales model, apply my manager's feedback the minute I get it, and track my own data and conversion. I own my own success. I create opportunities without being asked, and I do not wait for someone to tell me to move.
